title: Stop Wasting Your Tokens: Towards Efficient Runtime Multi-Agent Systems
one_liner: SupervisorAgent watches an agent system while it runs and steps in only at costly or error-prone moments, so the system spends less text budget while keeping task success steady.
lead: Multi-agent systems can solve long tasks, but they often keep talking when the next step is already clear or they continue after one wrong observation has pushed the run off course. This paper adds a small supervisor that monitors the live run, detects moments where the base system is drifting or overspending, and then gives a targeted correction. The key point is that supervision happens during the run, not after failure analysis, so the system can recover early and avoid needless extra turns.

problem.h2: The problem: long agent runs waste budget and spread mistakes
paras: A multi-agent system usually breaks a task into many steps: plan, search, read, discuss, write, and check. That flexibility helps on hard tasks because different agents can specialize on different subproblems, but it also creates a cost problem. Agents may repeat the same search, keep debating after the answer is already available, or continue reasoning from a bad observation. Each extra turn spends more text budget, and one bad step can contaminate several later steps because downstream agents trust the earlier result.

Most earlier work studies failure after the run ends. That helps diagnosis because it reveals the failure source, but it does not rescue the current attempt because the bad trajectory has already finished. The paper asks a stricter question: can we intervene at runtime, at the exact moment the run is going off track or becoming wasteful, without redesigning the whole agent system?

callout.b: The core idea in one sentence.
callout.html: Attach a lightweight supervisor that checks the live context with cheap filters and interrupts only when the base agents are wasting steps or acting on bad information.

panels.title: 1. Team starts the task
panels.caption: Several agents split the task and begin working in parallel.

panels.title: 2. One bad observation enters
panels.caption: A wrong search result or weak plan starts steering later steps.

panels.title: 3. Cheap filter notices risk
panels.viz_args: Context filter: repeated search, unsupported claim, drift from task, rising spend
panels.caption: A non-LLM filter scans the run and flags a moment worth supervising.

panels.title: 4. Supervisor steps in
panels.caption: The supervisor corrects the observation or tells the team to stop the wasteful branch.

panels.title: 5. Team finishes with fewer turns
panels.caption: The run stays on task and uses fewer extra turns because the correction arrived early.

steps.b: Step 1: Let the base system run normally
steps.text: SupervisorAgent does not replace the existing planner, workers, or tools. It watches the messages, tool outputs, and task state while the original system continues to operate.

steps.b: Step 2: Apply a cheap context filter
steps.text: A lightweight filter checks for warning signs such as repeated actions, unsupported statements, or observations that conflict with the task goal. The filter is cheap so that the monitoring cost stays small.

steps.b: Step 3: Trigger supervision only when needed
steps.text: If the filter sees no issue, the run continues untouched. If it sees risk, the supervisor is called so that expensive intervention happens only on a small subset of turns.
The supervisor can purify an observation, redirect the next action, or stop a useless branch. That helps because the correction lands before more agents build on the bad step.

steps.b: Step 5: Measure cost and success together
steps.text: The paper reports both task success and total text spend, because a useful supervisor must save budget without lowering task completion.

object.h2: What changes: the runtime context, not the agent architecture
paras: The paper leaves the base multi-agent system intact. The new object is a monitored runtime context: the supervisor sees the recent conversation, tool traces, and task progress, then injects a short correction only when the cheap filter says it matters. That means the method is modular because you can wrap an existing system instead of rebuilding it.

hidden.name: How much benefit a supervisor turn is likely to add
paras: The important hidden quantity is not simply whether the current step is wrong. It is whether intervening now will prevent enough future waste or future error propagation to justify the extra supervision cost. A repeated search may look harmless on its own, but it matters because it can lead to many more redundant turns. A doubtful observation matters even more if several later agents will rely on it.
The context filter is a proxy for this hidden quantity. It looks for patterns that usually precede wasted computation or cascading mistakes, then asks for supervision at those points.

heat.caption: Darker cells are places where an intervention is more valuable because they are more likely to cause later waste or error spread.

reads.html: Intervene when one extra check now can prevent many bad turns later.
Use runtime signals from the current context to estimate whether supervision will reduce future cost or future failure enough to pay for itself.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: early correction blocks downstream waste
paras: The method works because multi-agent systems amplify both good and bad intermediate results. If one agent finds a strong piece of evidence, many later steps benefit. If one agent introduces a false claim or a useless line of work, many later steps may also inherit that mistake. Runtime supervision acts at the branching point where a small correction can influence the entire later trajectory.

The cheap filter matters because constant supervision would erase the savings. By screening for only the turns that show clear warning patterns, the system spends supervision effort where it has the highest expected return. The reported gain comes from two effects together: fewer unnecessary turns and fewer runs that collapse after misinformation.

stages.s: Agents search, plan, and exchange findings
Cheap filter scans the live context
Supervisor triggers only on risky turns
Correction removes drift or repeated work
Similar success with lower total spend

math.h2: The main trade-off: save more future cost than you spend on supervision
math.words: A simple way to view the method is to compare the cost of supervision with the future cost it avoids. Intervene only when the expected saved cost from stopping drift, repeated work, or misinformation is larger than the extra cost of checking and correcting the run.
symbols: the expected later cost that disappears because the supervisor corrected the run early
the extra cost of running the filter and issuing a supervisor message
the total benefit of intervening at this point

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one branch is about to repeat three search-and-discussion turns that usually cost 120 units each.
Expected future waste without intervention = 3 x 120 = 360.
Calling the supervisor and issuing a correction costs 70 units.
The intervention is worthwhile because it removes much more future cost than it adds now.

math.note: The paper's main measured result fits this picture: runtime checks help because they are cheap and because they fire mostly on places where later waste would have been larger.

bars.h2: The payoff: lower spend, similar success

charts.title: Base multi-agent run
charts.note: Without runtime supervision, the system often keeps exploring after the useful evidence is already available.

charts.title: SupervisorAgent
charts.note: On GAIA, the paper reports about 29.68% lower spend without hurting success, because the supervisor removes costly drift while leaving successful runs mostly untouched.

items.html: If the cheap filter only catches obvious loops, the supervisor arrives too late. The system then pays the monitoring cost without blocking the hardest errors.

If the trigger is too sensitive, supervision cost grows and the base agents lose momentum. The method only saves budget when most ordinary turns pass through untouched because then supervision cost stays concentrated on the few branches where later waste would have been larger.

items.b: The supervisor gives a vague correction.
items.html: A correction must change the next action clearly. If it only restates the task, later agents may continue the same bad branch.

items.b: Done right: targeted checks save future work.
items.html: The method succeeds when the filter identifies high-value intervention points and the supervisor fixes them in a way that prevents several later wasteful turns.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small research assistant with a planner, a search worker, and a writer. Give it a set of tasks where one wrong web snippet or one repeated search tends to derail the run. Run the system once without supervision and record total spend, repeated actions, and task success. Then wrap the same system with a cheap trigger that watches for repeated actions and unsupported statements, and call a supervisor only on flagged turns. The demo should show that the supervised version uses less budget because it cuts off wasteful branches early, while task success stays similar because the base system still handles the normal parts of the task.
demo.metric_eq: Cost reduction = (base_spend - supervised_spend) / base_spend, tracked alongside task success on the same task set.
demo.closing: The demo must show two things at once: the supervisor lowers total spend and it does not buy that saving by simply giving up on hard tasks.
